title: Did It Happen: The Case for the Resurrection
subtitle: A five-session study weighing the historical case for the resurrection of Jesus, written toward the skeptic.
summary:
This study is for the doubter who has decided the resurrection is a beautiful story and nothing more, for the Christian who has never been told there is anything to say to that doubter beyond believe harder, and for the leader willing to host a room where both can speak without flinching. It walks the central claim of the Christian faith straight into the place it is most often dismissed, the question of whether it happened, and it refuses to pretend the question is rude. It is the most important question there is. If a man was dead and then was not, everything changes. If he was not, then Paul himself said our faith is worthless, and he said it first, before any skeptic thought to.

The study moves through five sessions. What the first Christians actually claimed, and the stakes they nailed it to. The historical bedrock that even the most critical scholars grant, and what it costs to grant it. The natural alternatives, each taken at full strength and tested rather than mocked. The strange, awkward detail of the women at the tomb, and why an inventor would never have written it. And finally, the weight of it, the firstfruits of a new creation, the hinge on which history turns, if it is true.

This is not a study that will hand anyone certainty in a box. It cannot, because history does not deal in proofs, only in probabilities weighed honestly. What it offers instead is a case strong enough that a thinking person can rest some weight on it without surrendering their mind. The writer came to faith from atheism, and he did not arrive by feeling. He arrived by being unable, finally, to explain the evidence any other way, and even then with doubt still in the room. He is not standing outside the skeptic's position lecturing it. He held it. He argued it. He is writing back to the man he used to be.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, skeptics, and seekers

sessions.title: The Claim That Will Not Die
sessions.aim: To hear what the first Christians actually claimed, stripped of familiarity, and to feel the full weight of the stakes they staked it on, so that the rest of the study has something real to weigh, while conceding from the start that a man rising from the dead is an extraordinary claim that deserves an extraordinary scrutiny.
sessions.summary: We have heard the word resurrection so often it has gone soft, worn down into a season and a sunrise service and a pastel banner. So begin by hearing it as a stranger would. The first Christians did not claim that Jesus lived on in their hearts, or that his teaching survived him, or that they had found a deeper symbolic truth in his death. They claimed that a man who was publicly executed and buried was, three days later, bodily alive, that they ate with him and touched him and watched him do the things the living do. The first question is whether we have any idea how strange that is. Bell takes the skeptic's instinct at full strength, because it is the right instinct. Extraordinary claims demand extraordinary evidence. Dead men do not rise, in our experience and in theirs, and a person who refuses to believe this on the first telling is not being closed-minded, they are being sane. He grants every bit of that. But then he shows what the first Christians did with the claim, which is the thing that should stop a careful skeptic. They did not hold it loosely as inspiration. They staked everything on whether it happened. Paul wrote that if Christ has not been raised, the whole faith is empty, a lie, a waste, and the dead are simply dead. No religion talks like that about its own founding miracle unless it believes the miracle is a fact that could, in principle, be checked. The turn is this. The resurrection is not offered as a moral or a metaphor. It is offered as an event, with a date and witnesses, and an event can be investigated. That is the wager of this whole study.

keyScripture.why: And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain, the moment Paul stakes the entire faith on a single historical event and invites it to be tested rather than merely believed, naming the resurrection as a fact that could in principle be falsified rather than a symbol immune to evidence.

discussion.q: Before any argument, say it honestly. When you hear the claim that a dead man walked out of a tomb, what is your gut reaction, and where do you think that reaction comes from?
discussion.behind: Surface the instinct before any case is made. For the skeptic it is disbelief, for the long-time believer it may be a worn familiarity that no longer registers the strangeness. The aim is to wake both up to how extraordinary the claim is, because a claim you have stopped hearing you cannot honestly weigh. Let the disbelief be spoken without correction.

discussion.q: Bell concedes that refusing to believe a resurrection on first hearing is not closed-minded but sane, because dead men do not rise. Does it change anything for you that the study starts by granting your doubt rather than scolding it?
discussion.behind: Establish the posture of the whole study, that the skeptic's instinct is honored, not attacked. The aim is to lower defenses so a real weighing can happen. A person braced for a lecture cannot think. Show that the case does not need the skeptic to be naive, it can afford to grant that dead men stay dead and still ask what happened here.

discussion.q: The first Christians did not claim Jesus lived on in their hearts or that his teaching survived. They claimed a body was alive again. Why does it matter that the claim is physical and specific rather than spiritual and vague?
discussion.behind: Press on the concreteness. Vague claims cannot be tested, physical ones can. The aim is to feel that the early Christians made the harder, riskier, more checkable claim, not the safer symbolic one, which is strange behavior for inventors who could have made it unfalsifiable instead.

discussion.q: Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, the whole faith is worthless and we are still in our sins. Why would the founder of a movement build in a clause that could destroy it, and what does that tell you about how he held the claim?
discussion.behind: Get the room to notice the falsifiability. Paul stakes everything on a fact, hands his critics the exact lever to topple the faith. The aim is to feel that this is not how people talk about a myth they invented, it is how people talk about an event they believe actually occurred and could be checked.

discussion.q: Bell says he held the skeptic's position himself, argued it, and did not leave it by feeling but by being unable to explain the evidence away. Where in your own thinking have you assumed the resurrection could not be examined, only believed or rejected?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication and to the central wager. Many on both sides assume faith and evidence are separate rooms. The aim is to name that assumption and set it aside for the study, to agree to treat the claim as an event that can be investigated, which is what the first Christians themselves did.

objections.objection: A man rising from the dead is an extraordinary claim, and extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. No amount of old testimony could ever clear that bar, so the whole question is settled before it starts. Dead men stay dead.
objections.response: Take the principle as stated, because it is a good principle and Bell will not pretend otherwise. Extraordinary claims do require extraordinary evidence, and dead men staying dead is precisely why the disciples themselves did not believe it at first, why Thomas demanded to touch the wounds, why the women came to the tomb expecting a corpse to anoint. They were not credulous peasants primed to believe in risings. They knew, as well as you do, that this does not happen. So grant the bar, and then notice what the principle actually requires. It requires that the evidence be weighed, not that the conclusion be ruled out in advance. If extraordinary evidence could never in principle count, then the principle is not a standard of inquiry, it is a refusal of inquiry wearing the costume of one. The honest form of your demand is this: show me evidence extraordinary enough to make the resurrection the best explanation of the facts, better than every natural alternative. That is a fair demand, and it is exactly the demand this study sets out to meet. It does not ask you to lower the bar. It asks you to actually hold the evidence up to it.

objections.objection: Every ancient religion has miracle stories, dying and rising gods, virgin births, divine visitations. The resurrection is just one more myth in a crowded field, and there is no reason to treat it differently from the rest.
objections.response: The comparison sounds devastating until you hold the stories side by side, and Bell asks you to actually do that rather than wave at the category. The dying-and-rising god myths are, almost without exception, cyclical and cosmic, tied to the seasons, set in a sacred once-upon-a-time, with no claim that a nameable man died under a nameable governor in a datable year and was seen alive by people you could go and question. The resurrection claim is the opposite kind of claim. It names Pontius Pilate, who really governed Judea. It names a public execution outside a real city. It names named witnesses, many still alive when the claim was first written down and circulated, who could be interrogated. The early Christians were not offering a myth about the renewal of nature. They were making a historical assertion about a particular Tuesday, give or take, in a particular spring. You may still conclude they were wrong. But the claim does not belong in the genre of myth, because myths do not invite you to go check the witnesses, and this one does. That difference is not decoration. It is the whole reason the question is worth a study.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If it turned out, beyond your ability to explain it away, that a man really did rise from the dead, what in your life would you most need to stay the same, and why?
sessions.practice: This week, before any of the evidence is weighed, sit with the claim itself in its full strangeness. Each day, read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly, and notice that Paul does not defend the resurrection as a comfort or a symbol but stakes the entire faith on it as a fact that could be false. Write down, honestly, what you would have to believe is true about the world for the resurrection to be impossible in principle, not merely unlikely. Then write down what evidence, if it existed, would actually move you. The aim is not to decide yet. It is to find out whether your mind is open enough to weigh anything, before the weighing begins.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, if you are there, some of us in this room are not sure, and we are not going to pretend otherwise, because pretending would dishonor both you and the truth. We have heard this claim so often that some of us stopped hearing it, and others of us never believed it for a moment. Tonight we ask only for honesty, ours and each other's. Give us minds willing to weigh what we have dismissed and hearts willing to be surprised. If a man rose, we want to know it. If he did not, we do not want to build our lives on a lie. Lead us toward what is true, wherever it takes us. Amen.
reflection: Have I ever actually examined the resurrection as a historical claim, or have I only ever accepted it or dismissed it as a matter of belief or unbelief?
What would have to be true about the world for the resurrection to be impossible in principle, and am I as sure of that as I assume I am?
If the first Christians staked everything on whether it happened, am I willing to treat the question with the same seriousness, knowing the answer might cost me something either way?
sessions.teaching: Begin by hearing the claim as if you had never heard it, because most of us have heard it so often that it no longer lands. The word resurrection has been worn smooth by repetition, softened into a season, a sunrise, a lily, a pastel banner over a church door once a year. We have to scrape all of that off and hear what the first Christians were actually saying, in the raw, because the familiarity has hidden the scandal. They were not saying that Jesus lived on in the memory of his followers. They were not saying his teaching outlasted his death, the way Socrates outlasted his. They were not saying they had found, in his execution, a deeper symbolic truth about sacrifice or love or the renewal of the world. They were saying something far more specific, far stranger, and far more dangerous. They were saying that a man who had been publicly tortured to death and sealed in a tomb was, on the third day, bodily alive. Not a ghost. Not a vision that faded. They claimed to have eaten with him, touched him, watched him do the ordinary things only the living do. And the first question I want to put to this room, before any evidence is weighed, is whether we have the faintest idea how strange that is. Take the skeptic's instinct now, and take it at its full strength, because it is the right instinct and I will not insult it. Dead men do not rise. This is the most reliable fact in human experience. It was as true in the first century as it is in this room. The skeptic who hears the claim and refuses to believe it on the first telling is not being closed-minded or willfully blind. He is being sane. Carl Sagan put the principle in its sharpest modern form, that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and I grant it completely, without reservation, because the principle is correct. A claim this far outside ordinary experience cannot be accepted on a shrug or a feeling or a tradition. It has to clear a very high bar. I held that position myself, for years. I came to faith out of atheism, and I did not arrive by sentiment or by a warm feeling at a service. I argued against this claim. I assumed, as many honest people do, that it was the kind of thing you either believed or you did not, a matter of the heart and not of the evidence, sealed off in a private compartment where reasons do not reach. So I am not standing outside the skeptic's position lecturing it from a safe distance. I lived inside it. I am writing back to the man I used to be. But here is the thing that finally cracked that compartment open for me, and it is the thing I want to set before you tonight, because it is strange, and the strangeness is the point. Watch what the first Christians did with this claim. They did not hold it the way you hold an inspiration, loosely, comfortably, immune to disproof. They staked everything on whether it actually happened. Listen to Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, almost certainly within twenty-five years of the event, to a community that included people who would have wanted to argue. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. He is not finished. We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. And then the line that should stop any careful skeptic cold. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. Notice what Paul has done. He has built into the foundation of the entire faith a clause that could destroy it. He has handed his critics the exact lever they would need to topple the whole structure. If you can show the resurrection did not happen, he says, then I am a liar, your faith is worthless, your dead are simply dead, and you have wasted your life believing me. No one talks like this about a myth they invented. No one builds a falsification clause into their own founding miracle unless they believe the miracle is a fact, a thing that happened in the world, a thing that could in principle be checked by going and asking the people who were there. The mythmaker makes his claim unfalsifiable, sets it safely in the realm of the symbolic where no evidence can reach it. Paul did the opposite. He set the claim down in history, with a date, a place, a governor's name, and a list of named witnesses, most of them still alive, and he all but dared the reader to go check. So here is the verdict this first session leaves us with, and it is not a proof of anything yet. It is a reframing of the whole question. The resurrection is not offered to you, in the New Testament, as a moral lesson or a beautiful metaphor or a private comfort that asks only to be believed. It is offered as an event. An event has a time and a place and witnesses. And an event can be investigated. You do not have to decide tonight whether it happened. But you do have to decide whether you are willing to treat it as the kind of thing that can be weighed, evidence on the scale, alternatives honestly considered, the best explanation pursued wherever it leads. That is the wager of this entire study, and it is the wager the first Christians made first. They did not ask you to feel the resurrection. They asked you to reckon with it. So do not believe it tonight. I am not asking you to. I am asking you to stop assuming it cannot be examined, and to bring your full skepticism with you when we begin, next session, to actually weigh what we have.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the difference between an event and a myth, because the whole posture of this study depends on it and the modern reflex is to file the resurrection under myth without examining the category. Scholars of comparative religion have long noted that the so-called dying-and-rising gods of the ancient world, figures like Osiris or Adonis, function within the cycle of the seasons and the fertility of the land, set in a primordial time outside ordinary history, with no claim that a particular man died on a particular date and was seen alive afterward by nameable people. The resurrection claim is structurally different. N. T. Wright, in his major historical study The Resurrection of the Son of God, published in 2003, argues at length that the early Christian belief is not a development of pagan myth and not a natural outgrowth of Jewish expectation either, since first-century Judaism expected a general resurrection of all the righteous at the end of history, not the resurrection of one man in the middle of it. The Christian claim was a strange mutation within Jewish hope, not borrowed from the pagans and not predicted by the Jews, and that strangeness itself calls for explanation. Set this beside the assumption, common since the nineteenth century, that early Christianity simply absorbed surrounding mystery religions, an assumption that has steadily lost ground as the actual texts have been compared more carefully and the chronology examined. A serious group should ask what it would take for a claim to count as historical rather than mythical, and then ask honestly which category the New Testament resurrection claim actually fits, given its named witnesses, its public setting, and its built-in invitation to be checked. The discipline of this session is simply to refuse the easy filing, to hold the claim long enough to feel its strangeness, and to agree, before weighing any evidence, that it is the kind of claim that can be weighed at all.

sessions.title: The Minimal Facts
sessions.aim: To lay out the small set of historical facts that even the most critical, including skeptical and non-Christian, scholars grant, and to feel the strange weight of those facts standing together, while steelmanning the leading skeptic at full strength rather than the weakest version of unbelief.
sessions.summary: You do not have to trust the Bible as the inspired word of God to ask the historical question, and this session deliberately does not ask you to. It works instead from a short list of facts that almost the entire field of scholarship, believing and unbelieving alike, accepts on ordinary historical grounds. Gary Habermas built much of his career mapping exactly this consensus, what he called the minimal facts, the data granted even by scholars with no stake in the conclusion. The first question is what those facts are. That Jesus was executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is granted by nearly everyone, including the most skeptical historians, because it is attested everywhere and no one invents a crucified messiah. That the disciples sincerely believed they saw him alive afterward is granted, because they said so under threat and died saying it. That Paul, a violent persecutor of the church, was abruptly converted by what he was sure was an encounter with the risen Jesus, is granted, because Paul tells us himself in letters everyone dates early. That James, Jesus' own skeptical brother, who did not believe during Jesus' life, became a leader of the church and died for it, is granted. And that a creed naming the resurrection and its witnesses was already circulating within a few years of the crucifixion, preserved in 1 Corinthians 15, is granted by critical scholars across the spectrum. Bell steelmans the skeptic at full strength here, in the person of Bart Ehrman, who grants most of these facts and still does not believe, and whose reasons deserve a fair hearing. The turn is not that the facts prove the resurrection. It is that the facts are real, agreed, and stubborn, and that any honest explanation, including the skeptic's, now has to account for all of them at once.

keyScripture.why: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared, an early creed Paul says he received and passed on, dated by critical scholars to within a few years of the crucifixion, far too early for legend to account for it.

discussion.q: This session works only from facts that even skeptical, non-Christian historians grant, without asking you to trust the Bible as inspired. Does it change how you weigh the question to know the case does not depend on faith in Scripture first?
discussion.behind: Establish the method up front. Many assume the case for the resurrection requires accepting the Bible as the word of God, which lets them dismiss it as circular. The aim is to feel that the minimal facts are granted on ordinary historical grounds across the field, so the question can be weighed even by someone who trusts no part of the Bible.

discussion.q: Even the most skeptical historians grant that the disciples sincerely believed they saw Jesus alive, and many of them died holding to it. Liars make poor martyrs. What weight do you give to the fact that they suffered for a claim they could have known was false?
discussion.behind: Press on sincerity versus truth. The point is narrow and must stay narrow, that the disciples were not knowing liars, since people do not die for what they know they made up. This does not prove the resurrection, only rules out deliberate fraud. Keep the room from overclaiming while feeling the genuine weight of the martyrdoms.

discussion.q: Paul was a violent enemy of the church, and James was Jesus' own brother who did not believe during his lifetime. Both became leaders willing to die for the claim. Why are converted enemies and skeptical family harder to explain than enthusiastic followers?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel why hostile and skeptical witnesses carry extra weight. Followers might be expected to believe, but an enemy and a doubting brother had every reason not to. The aim is to see that something turned them, and that whatever it was has to be accounted for by any explanation, including a skeptical one.

discussion.q: The creed in 1 Corinthians 15 is dated by critical scholars to within a few years of the crucifixion, too early for legend to grow. Why does the early date of the claim matter so much to whether it could be a slowly invented legend?
discussion.behind: Press on chronology against the legend theory. Legends need generations, and the creed is too early for that. The aim is to feel that the resurrection claim was not a late embellishment but was already fixed and circulating almost immediately, which sharply limits how much the legend explanation can carry, an argument developed fully next session.

discussion.q: Bell presents Bart Ehrman, a skeptic who grants most of these facts and still does not believe, at full strength rather than knocking down a weaker doubter. Why does it matter that the study argues against the strongest version of unbelief rather than the easiest?
discussion.behind: Close on the discipline of steelmanning. A case that only beats a weak skeptic has proven little. The aim is to honor the room's hardest doubts by facing the best skeptical mind honestly, and to feel that the facts are strong precisely because even those who grant them can still resist the conclusion, which keeps the study honest about what the facts do and do not establish.

objections.objection: Bart Ehrman grants that the disciples had experiences they believed were the risen Jesus, and he is one of the most respected New Testament scholars alive, and he does not believe in the resurrection. If a leading expert who knows all of this remains a skeptic, why should I conclude otherwise?
objections.response: Bell takes Ehrman seriously, by name and at full strength, because he is exactly the right person to reckon with, a scholar who knows the evidence as well as anyone and lands on the other side. So hear what Ehrman actually grants and where he actually stands, without softening it. Ehrman grants that Jesus was crucified, that the disciples sincerely believed they saw him alive, that the church exploded out of that conviction. What he does not grant is the inference to a miracle, and his stated reason is principled, not careless: he argues that the historian, working as a historian, cannot affirm a miracle, because the historian deals in probabilities and a miracle is by definition the least probable event, so the most improbable explanation can never be the best historical explanation. That is a serious argument and it deserves a serious answer, not a sneer. Here is the answer. Ehrman has not weighed the resurrection against the alternatives and found it wanting. He has ruled it out before weighing, by a rule that defines miracle as inadmissible from the start. That is a philosophical commitment, not a historical finding. If you grant that a miracle is impossible before you look, then of course the evidence can never get you there, but then it was never the evidence deciding, it was the rule. The honest question is not whether a historian qua historian may affirm a miracle. It is whether, with that rule set aside, the resurrection is the best explanation of the facts Ehrman himself grants. He has not shown that it is not. He has declined to ask.

objections.objection: People die for false beliefs all the time. Muslims, Mormons, members of every cult have died for what they believed, and they were sincere and they were wrong. The willingness of the disciples to die proves nothing except that they were sincere, which everyone already knew.
objections.response: This is the strongest form of the objection and it is right about almost everything, so hear exactly where it holds and where it does not. You are entirely correct that sincerity does not prove truth. People die for false beliefs constantly, and the disciples being willing to die does not, by itself, mean the resurrection happened. Bell grants that fully, and any honest case has to. But notice the precise and narrow thing the martyrdoms actually establish, which is smaller than truth and larger than nothing. The modern martyrs you name, sincere and wrong, are dying for things they believe on someone else's testimony, a revelation received by a founder, a doctrine handed down. They are in the position of believing a claim. The disciples were in a different position. They were not dying for something they had been told. They were dying for something they claimed to have seen with their own eyes, a body, alive, that they touched and ate with. A person can die sincerely for a false belief they received. It is far harder to die for a thing you claim to have personally witnessed if you know you witnessed no such thing. So the martyrdoms do not prove the resurrection. What they do is close off one specific explanation, the oldest and simplest one, that the disciples knew it was false and lied anyway. Liars make poor martyrs. That leaves the field to the sincere explanations, and those we will weigh, every one, next session.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which of these facts, if you sat with it honestly, is hardest for you to fit into the story you currently believe about how Christianity began, and why that one?
sessions.practice: This week, take the minimal facts one at a time, one per day, and treat each as a historian would, not as a believer or a skeptic but as someone trying to account for the data. Write each fact at the top of a page: Jesus was crucified, the disciples believed they saw him alive, Paul the persecutor converted, James the skeptic converted, the early creed was circulating within a few years. Under each, write the best natural explanation you can think of, the most reasonable account that does not involve a resurrection. Do not strain to make them fail. Make them as strong as you honestly can. The aim is to feel, by the end of the week, whether the natural explanations grow easier or harder as the facts are made to stand together, which sets up the work of the next session.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of truth, if these facts are stubborn, let us not flinch from them, and if our explanations are thin, let us not pretend they are thick. We do not want a faith built on bad history, and we do not want an unbelief built on a rule that decided the answer before it looked. Give us the patience to hold the evidence honestly, the humility to follow it where it leads, and the courage to let it cost us our certainty, whichever certainty it is. For those of us who do not believe, keep us honest skeptics and not lazy ones. For those of us who do, keep our faith from resting on arguments we have not actually examined. Lead us toward what really happened. Amen.

sessions.teaching: Here is the move that changed how I thought about this, back when I was the one arguing against it. You do not have to believe the Bible is the inspired word of God to ask the historical question. For years I assumed you did, that the whole case for the resurrection rested on first accepting Scripture as divinely authoritative, which made the argument circular and let me dismiss it without effort. Believe the Bible because the Bible says to. But that is not how serious historians work, and it is not how this session works. We are going to set the question of inspiration entirely aside and work only from facts that the broad field of scholarship, believing and unbelieving alike, grants on ordinary historical grounds, the same grounds they would use for any event in the ancient world. Gary Habermas spent much of his career mapping precisely this, surveying the scholarship and identifying what he called the minimal facts, the data conceded even by scholars who have no stake whatsoever in the Christian conclusion, often a stake against it. Let me lay them out, because their power is cumulative, and it is the cumulative weight that matters. First, Jesus was executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. This is granted by virtually everyone, including the most hostile critics, because it is attested in multiple independent sources inside and outside the New Testament, and because, frankly, it is the last thing the early church would have invented. A crucified messiah was a contradiction in terms, a scandal, a stumbling block, as Paul himself admits. You do not make up the most embarrassing possible fact about your founder. The crucifixion is bedrock. Second, the disciples sincerely believed they saw Jesus alive after his death. Note the careful wording. Not that he rose, that is the conclusion we are testing, but that they sincerely believed they encountered him alive. This too is granted across the spectrum, by skeptics included, because the disciples said so under threat, proclaimed it in the very city where he had been executed weeks earlier, and a number of them died holding to it. And here we must be precise, because the point is easy to overstate and easy to dismiss. Sincerity does not prove truth. People die for false beliefs all the time. What the martyrdoms establish is narrower and harder to escape. The disciples were not dying for a doctrine they received from someone else. They were dying for something they claimed to have personally seen, a body, alive, touched, eaten with. And a person can die sincerely for a falsehood they were told, but it is a very different thing to die for a thing you claim to have witnessed yourself when you know you witnessed no such thing. Liars make poor martyrs. So the simplest, oldest explanation, that the disciples knew it was false and lied, runs aground here. Whatever happened, they were not knowing frauds. Third, Paul. Saul of Tarsus was not a sympathetic follower waiting to believe. He was a violent enemy of the church, by his own account, present at the killing of Stephen, hunting Christians from house to house. And then, abruptly, he was on the other side, the movement's most relentless missionary, suffering beatings and imprisonment and finally death for the very faith he had tried to destroy, and he tells us himself, in letters no serious scholar disputes, that the reason was an encounter he was certain was the risen Jesus. A converted enemy is hard to explain away. He had every motive to stay an enemy and none to switch. Fourth, James, the brother of Jesus. The gospels record, with the same awkward honesty that records the disciples' failures, that Jesus' own family did not believe in him during his lifetime, that his brothers thought him out of his mind. And yet after the crucifixion, James is suddenly a leader of the Jerusalem church, and the early historian Josephus records that he was put to death for his faith. Something turned a skeptical brother into a martyr. Skeptical family, like converted enemies, do not flip for no reason. Fifth, and this is the one that does the most work, the creed. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul writes: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive. Notice the language. Delivered and received are the technical terms for handing on a fixed tradition, and the formulaic structure marks this as a creed Paul did not compose but inherited, learned, and is repeating. Critical scholars across the spectrum, including skeptics, date this creed extraordinarily early, to within a few years of the crucifixion, some within months, traced to Paul's own contact with the Jerusalem apostles. This matters enormously, and we will press it next session, because legends need time, generations of retelling, and this is not a legend that grew over centuries. This is a fixed claim, naming witnesses, circulating almost immediately, while the witnesses were alive to be questioned. Now, I promised to take the skeptic at full strength, and I mean the strongest skeptic, not the easiest. Bart Ehrman is one of the most respected New Testament scholars alive, and he is not a believer. And here is the honest and important thing: Ehrman grants most of these facts. He grants the crucifixion. He grants that the disciples sincerely believed they saw Jesus alive. He grants the explosive birth of the church out of that conviction. What he does not grant is the leap to a miracle, and his reason is not laziness, it is principled. He argues that a historian, working strictly as a historian, cannot affirm a miracle, because the historian's craft is the weighing of probabilities, and a miracle is by definition the least probable thing that could happen, so the most improbable explanation can never be the most probable, and therefore can never be the best historical conclusion. That is a serious argument, and I will not wave it away, because a great many thoughtful skeptics hold some version of it. But look closely at what it actually does. Ehrman has not weighed the resurrection against the natural alternatives and found a better natural explanation. He has ruled the resurrection out before the weighing begins, by a rule that defines miracle as inadmissible from the start. And that is a philosophical commitment, not a historical discovery. If you decide in advance that a miracle is the one explanation never allowed on the table, then of course the evidence can never seat it there, but then it was never the evidence that decided, it was the rule you brought to the evidence. So here is the verdict this session leaves us with, and I want to state it exactly, no more and no less. The minimal facts do not prove the resurrection. I am not claiming they do. What they do is stand there, real, agreed, stubborn, and refuse to be wished away, and they hand every explanation the same hard assignment. Whatever account you reach for, miracle or natural, must explain all of them at once. The crucifixion. The disciples' sincere conviction. The converted enemy. The skeptical brother. The creed too early for legend. Any honest person, believer or skeptic, now owes the facts a single explanation that fits them all. We have closed the door on fraud. Next session, we open every other door there is, the hallucination, the legend, the swoon, the stolen body, the wrong tomb, and we test each one at full strength, the way the facts demand.

scriptureStudy.note: I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died, that he was buried, that he was raised, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Delivered and received are technical terms for handing on fixed tradition, marking this as an inherited creed, not Paul's composition.

Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Paul names living witnesses who could be questioned, an invitation to verification that a legend would not extend.

Last of all he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, because I persecuted the church of God. Paul records his own past as an enemy of the church, the converted persecutor testifying against his own former interest.

You have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. Paul confirms in an undisputed early letter that he was a violent enemy before his conversion, making the turn harder to explain naturally.

And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, He is out of his mind. The gospels record, with embarrassing honesty, that Jesus' own family did not believe in him during his lifetime, setting up the weight of James's later conversion.

For not even his brothers believed in him. The skepticism of Jesus' brothers is stated plainly, which makes James's emergence as a leader of the church and his death for the faith a fact in need of explanation.

Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed. Paul insists the message he preaches is the same as that of the original apostles, a unified and early testimony rather than a later divergence or invention.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the dating of the creed in 1 Corinthians 15, because it is the single most consequential piece of the minimal-facts case and the place where careful work pays off. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians around the middle of the first century, but he says he is passing on something he himself received, using the technical vocabulary of tradition, which means the creed predates the letter, perhaps by decades. Many scholars, including critical ones, trace its origin to Paul's early contact with the apostles in Jerusalem, described in Galatians, within a handful of years of the crucifixion, and some argue the core formula was already in use within months. The significance is chronological. The standard skeptical account of miracle stories is that they accrue over generations as a figure is gradually elevated by his admirers, the historical man buried under layers of legendary embellishment. That account requires time, the slow work of retelling across communities that no longer remember the facts firsthand. A creed circulating within a few years, naming living witnesses, simply does not give legend the room it needs. Gary Habermas built his minimal-facts approach precisely on this kind of early and widely conceded data, arguing that one should rest the case only on facts granted by the great majority of scholars across the believing and skeptical spectrum, so that the conclusion does not depend on contested or distinctly Christian premises. Set this beside the older liberal assumption, dominant in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, that the resurrection accounts were late developments, and notice how the early dating of the creed has reshaped the scholarly conversation. A serious group should weigh both halves honestly: the early date is a genuine problem for the legend theory, but the minimal-facts method also has its critics, who argue that consensus is not the same as truth and that granting the facts is not granting the inference. Hold both. The facts are early and widely conceded. The inference from the facts is exactly what the rest of the study must earn.

sessions.title: The Alternatives, Honestly Weighed
sessions.aim: To take each natural explanation of the facts in turn, state it in the strongest form its own defenders would recognize, and then test it against the evidence, refusing the cheap dismissal, so that whatever the room concludes is reached by weighing and not by mockery.
sessions.summary: If the disciples were not lying, and the facts are real, then something happened, and the honest skeptic has natural explanations ready. This session does not laugh at them. It builds each one at its strongest, the way its defenders would, and then asks whether it actually accounts for all the facts at once. The hallucination theory, that the grieving disciples saw what they longed to see, is the most serious, and Bell gives it its full weight before noting that hallucinations are private and individual while the appearances were repeatedly to groups, and that grief does not convert enemies like Paul or skeptics like James. The legend theory, that the story grew over time, runs into the creed of 1 Corinthians 15, too early for legend to form. The swoon theory, that Jesus survived the cross, asks us to believe that a flogged and crucified and speared man not only survived but, days later in a sealed tomb, freed himself and convinced his followers he was the conqueror of death rather than a man in desperate need of a physician. The stolen body, by the disciples, returns us to liars who then died for the lie, and by anyone else, leaves the disciples' sincere experiences unexplained. The wrong tomb, that they simply went to the wrong place, founders on the fact that the authorities, motivated to produce the body, never did. The turn is honest and humble. None of these is impossible. Each is conceivable in isolation. But the question history asks is not what is possible. It is what is the best explanation of all the facts together, and that is the scale on which the resurrection must be weighed, fairly, against its rivals.

keyScripture.why: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, the appearance to a large group at once that the private and individual nature of hallucination struggles to explain, and the named living witnesses that the slow growth of legend cannot accommodate.

discussion.q: This session builds each skeptical explanation at its strongest before testing it, rather than mocking it. Why is steelmanning the alternatives, refusing the cheap dismissal, essential if the conclusion is going to mean anything?
discussion.behind: Establish the discipline first. A case that only beats a straw version of the alternatives has proven nothing. The aim is to commit the room to honesty, to feel that a conclusion reached by mocking the rivals is worthless, and that the resurrection is only worth believing if it survives the strongest natural explanations, not the weakest.

discussion.q: The hallucination theory is the most serious alternative, that grieving disciples saw what they longed to see. Where is it genuinely strong, and where does the fact that the appearances were repeatedly to groups, and even to enemies, strain it?
discussion.behind: Take the strongest rival seriously. Grief does produce vivid experiences, and the theory deserves real weight. The aim is to feel both its force and its limits, that hallucinations are private and individual while the appearances were to groups and to hostile witnesses like Paul, which grief does not easily explain.

discussion.q: The swoon theory says Jesus survived the cross and revived in the tomb. Stated strongly, it removes the miracle entirely. What has to be true for it to work, and does the condition a survivor would be in match a man his followers called the conqueror of death?
discussion.behind: Press on the swoon theory's internal strain. To work, a flogged, crucified, speared man must survive, escape a sealed tomb, and convince followers he had conquered death. The aim is to feel that the survivor would have needed a physician, not been mistaken for the risen Lord of life, without mocking the theory, which is at least naturalistic.

discussion.q: The wrong-tomb theory says the disciples simply went to the wrong burial place. Why is the silence of the authorities, who were motivated to produce the body and end the movement, such a problem for this and for the stolen-body theory?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the weight of the missing body. If the tomb was wrong or the body stolen, the authorities had every reason and opportunity to produce the corpse and crush the claim in its infancy, and they did not. The aim is to see that the empty tomb is a problem the natural theories must explain, not assume away.

discussion.q: Bell concludes that none of the alternatives is impossible, only that history asks which is the best explanation of all the facts at once. Knowing he refuses to claim the resurrection is proven, does that honesty make the case more credible or less, for you?
discussion.behind: Close on the actual standard, best explanation rather than proof. History deals in probabilities, not certainties. The aim is to feel that the modesty of the claim, that the resurrection is the best explanation rather than a proven fact, is more honest and therefore more trustworthy than an overclaim, and to weigh the rivals on that fair scale themselves.

objections.objection: Grief makes people see things. Bereaved spouses see and hear their dead partners all the time, vividly, and believe it completely. The disciples loved Jesus and were devastated, and they saw what their grief produced. The hallucination theory explains the appearances without any miracle.
objections.response: This is the strongest natural explanation there is, and Bell gives it its full weight, because it is true that grief produces vivid and convincing experiences, and bereavement visions are well documented and real. So grant the theory its real force, and then ask whether it actually fits the facts we have, all of them. Two things strain it hard. First, hallucinations are by their nature private and individual events, generated by one mind, which is why two people do not share the same dream. The appearances in the earliest sources are repeatedly to groups, to the twelve together, to a gathering Paul numbers at more than five hundred. A shared grief might produce many individual experiences, but it does not produce one collective experience seen in common, the way a crowd cannot hallucinate the same external event. Second, and harder still, grief explains the disciples, who loved Jesus and longed to see him, but it does not explain Paul, who was not grieving but persecuting, and it does not explain James, the skeptical brother who did not believe. You do not hallucinate your way out of hostility into martyrdom. Bereavement visions comfort the grieving. They do not convert the enemy. The theory is strong where the witnesses loved him and silent where they did not.

objections.objection: Stories grow in the telling. A man dies, his followers honor him, and over the years the legend swells until an ordinary teacher becomes a risen god. That is how every religious legend forms, slowly, by embellishment, and the resurrection is no different.
objections.response: As a general account of how legends form, this is entirely correct, and Bell does not dispute it, legends do grow exactly this way, slowly, by accretion, over generations. The whole question is whether the resurrection had the time it would need, and the evidence says it did not. The claim that Jesus rose and appeared to named witnesses is not found only in late documents written long after the participants were gone. It is fixed in the creed of 1 Corinthians 15, which Paul says he received and is handing on, dated by critical scholars, skeptics among them, to within a few years of the crucifixion, while the witnesses it names were still alive. Legend needs the firsthand witnesses to die off so the embellishment has room to grow unchecked. Here the central claim is already fixed and circulating almost immediately, in the lifetime and the hometown of the people who could contradict it. So the legend theory does not fail because legends do not grow, they do. It fails because this particular claim was nailed down too early and too publicly for the slow work of legend to be what produced it. You would need the legend fully formed within a few years, among eyewitnesses, in the city of the events, which is not how legend works at all.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Of all the natural explanations, which one do you most want to be true, and is it the evidence that draws you to it, or the relief of not having to deal with what the other answer would ask of you?
sessions.practice: This week, take the five alternatives, one per day, and argue each one as if your reputation depended on defending it. Hallucination. Legend. Swoon. Stolen body. Wrong tomb. For each, write the strongest case you can build, the version its smartest defender would sign, and then, only after you have made it as strong as honestly possible, write down the facts from session two that it explains well and the ones it struggles with. Do not let yourself off easy on either side. The aim is to reach the end of the week having actually weighed each rival on the scale of all the facts at once, so that whatever you conclude, you conclude it by weighing and not by wanting, and you can say honestly why the explanation you favor is better than the ones you set aside.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of truth, we do not want to believe something because it comforts us, and we do not want to disbelieve something because it would cost us. Both are ways of lying to ourselves, and tonight we have tried to stop. Where we have reached for the easy explanation because the hard one frightened us, forgive us. Where we have mocked an answer instead of weighing it, forgive us that too. Give us the rare honesty to follow the evidence past our preferences, to grant what is strong in every account and to name what is weak, and to land where the facts actually lead rather than where we wish they did. If the best explanation is the one we have been avoiding, give us the courage to say so. Amen.
reflection: Which natural explanation did I assume settled the question before this session, and did it survive being stated at its strongest and tested against all the facts at once?
Where was I tempted to mock an alternative instead of weighing it, and what does that temptation reveal about whether I am seeking truth or defending a position?
If history asks for the best explanation rather than a proof, can I say honestly why the explanation I favor accounts for the facts better than the ones I am setting aside?
sessions.teaching: We ended the last session by closing one door. If the disciples were not lying, and the minimal facts are real and agreed, then something genuinely happened, and the honest skeptic does not throw up his hands, he reaches for a natural explanation. He should. That is exactly what a careful mind ought to do, look for the ordinary account before reaching for the extraordinary one. So tonight we are going to do something that a lot of Christian apologetics skips, to its shame. We are going to take each natural explanation in turn, build it at its strongest, in the form its own best defenders would recognize and sign, and only then ask whether it actually accounts for the facts. No mockery. No straw men. Because a case that only beats a weak version of the alternatives has proven nothing at all, and if the resurrection is true it can survive the strongest rivals, and if it cannot survive them, I do not want you to believe it. Start with the most serious one, the hallucination theory, because it is genuinely the best natural explanation and it deserves to be treated as such. The disciples loved Jesus. They were shattered by his death. Grief does strange and powerful things to the human mind, and we know this is not fantasy, because bereavement visions are extensively documented, real experiences in which grieving people see and hear and feel the presence of the one they lost, vividly enough to be utterly convinced. So the theory runs: the disciples, in the agony of loss and the longing to see him again, saw what their grief produced, and mistook it for the living Jesus. That is a strong theory. I have felt its pull. Now test it honestly against the facts, all of them. Two things strain it, one hard and one harder. The first is the nature of hallucination itself. Hallucinations are private events. They are generated inside a single mind, which is precisely why two people cannot share one, the way two people cannot share a dream. But the earliest sources do not describe a series of private individual visions. They describe appearances to groups, to the eleven gathered together, to a crowd Paul numbers at over five hundred at once. A roomful of grieving people might each have their own experience, but they do not collectively perceive the same external figure, hear the same words, watch the same hands. Grief is individual. The appearances, as reported, were corporate. The second strain is heavier still. Grief explains the people who were grieving, the disciples who loved him and ached for him. It does not explain Paul, who was not grieving but actively persecuting, who had no longing to see Jesus alive and every motive to want him dead and gone. And it does not explain James, the brother who, the sources tell us with embarrassing candor, did not believe during Jesus' lifetime. You do not hallucinate your way from enemy to apostle, from skeptic to martyr. Bereavement visions comfort those who loved the dead. They do not convert his enemies. So the hallucination theory is powerful exactly where the witnesses loved him, and goes silent exactly where they did not, and the facts include witnesses who did not. Next, the legend theory, that the resurrection story grew gradually in the telling, an ordinary teacher slowly elevated by his admirers until he became a risen god. As a general account of how legends form, this is simply correct, and I will not dispute it for a second. Legends do grow this way, by accretion, over generations, as the firsthand witnesses die off and the embellishment gains room to swell unchecked. The entire question is whether the resurrection had the time it would need, and we already saw, last session, that it did not. The claim is not confined to late documents written long after the participants were gone. It is fixed in the creed of 1 Corinthians 15, which Paul received and is passing on, dated by critical scholars within a few years of the crucifixion, naming witnesses who were still alive. Legend needs the eyewitnesses gone. This claim was nailed down while they were present, in the very city of the events, by people who could be contradicted. The legend theory does not fail because legends are not real. It fails because this legend would have had to form fully, within a few years, among the eyewitnesses, in the hometown of the crucifixion, and that is not how legend works. Then the swoon theory, which has the real virtue of being completely naturalistic. It proposes that Jesus did not actually die on the cross but lapsed into unconsciousness, was taken for dead, and later revived in the cool of the tomb. State it at full strength: misdiagnosed death is not unheard of, and a powerful constitution might endure more than expected. But follow it all the way through, soberly. This is a man who had been scourged with a Roman flagrum, nailed to a cross for hours, and, the sources add, pierced through the side with a spear by professional executioners whose own lives depended on confirming death. For the swoon theory to work, that man must not only have survived all of that, but must then, with no medical care, after days in a sealed tomb without food or water, have unwrapped himself, moved a heavy stone from the inside, overpowered or evaded a guard, and walked out, and then so convinced his followers of his vitality that they proclaimed him not a desperately wounded man in need of a physician but the risen conqueror of death itself. The condition such a survivor would actually be in is the exact opposite of the impression the appearances made. A half-dead man crawling out of a tomb inspires pity and a search for a doctor. He does not inspire a movement that conquers an empire on the claim that death has been beaten. The theory removes the miracle and replaces it with a different impossibility. Then the stolen body, in its two forms. If the disciples stole it, we are right back at the door we closed last session, liars who then suffered and died for what they knew to be a fraud, and we already saw that liars make poor martyrs. If someone else stole it, the authorities, grave robbers, anyone, then perhaps the tomb was empty, but the theft explains nothing about the appearances, the sincere experiences of the disciples and Paul and James, which the facts still demand an account of. An empty tomb with no appearances is not Christianity. The stolen body, by whoever, leaves the central data untouched. And finally the wrong tomb, the gentlest theory, that in the confusion and grief the women simply went to the wrong burial place, found it empty, and leapt to a conclusion. But this one founders on a single stubborn fact. The authorities, both Jewish and Roman, had every motive in the world to end this movement in its cradle, and the simplest way to end it, the moment the disciples began proclaiming a risen Jesus in Jerusalem, was to walk to the correct tomb, produce the body, and parade it through the streets. They never did. They could not. The wrong-tomb theory asks us to believe that the grieving women got the location wrong but the authorities, motivated and able, never managed to get it right. So here is the verdict, and I want to state it with real care, because the temptation now is to overclaim, and overclaiming would betray everything we have tried to do honestly. None of these alternatives is impossible. I will not say that, because it is not true. Each one, taken alone, in isolation, is conceivable. A determined skeptic can hold any single one of them. But that is not the question history asks. History never deals in proof or in impossibility. It deals in probability, in the weighing of explanations against the full body of evidence, and the question it asks is always the same: which account best explains all the facts together. Not the crucifixion alone, or the empty tomb alone, or the appearances alone, but the crucifixion and the empty tomb and the group appearances and the converted enemy and the skeptical brother and the creed too early for legend, all of it, at once, in one explanation. And when you put every natural theory on that scale, each one explains some of the facts and strains against others. The hallucination handles the appearances and stumbles on the enemies. The legend handles the development and stumbles on the early creed. The swoon handles the empty tomb and stumbles on the impossible survivor. The stolen body and wrong tomb handle the empty tomb and leave the appearances untouched. Every natural explanation is strong somewhere and breaks somewhere. The resurrection, whatever else you say about it, is the one explanation that, if granted, accounts for all of them at once. That is not a proof. I have not proven anything tonight, and I will not pretend I have. It is a claim about explanatory power, weighed on the only scale history offers, and it is the claim you now have to weigh for yourself, honestly, against rivals you have actually seen at their strongest. The door of fraud is closed. The natural doors are open but each one creaks. What remains is the weight of the whole, and what best bears it.

scriptureStudy.note: He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time. The appearance to a large group at once strains the hallucination theory, since hallucinations are private and individual and a crowd does not perceive the same external figure in common.

The chief priests devised a plan to say his disciples came by night and stole him away. The earliest counter-explanation is not that the tomb was full but that the body was taken, conceding the tomb was empty and shifting to theft, the stolen-body theory in its oldest form.

But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water. The death is confirmed by professional executioners, straining the swoon theory at its root.

But these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. The disciples did not credulously expect a resurrection but dismissed the first report as nonsense, which counts against the theory that wishful grief readily produced belief.

Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. Mary's first assumption is theft or relocation, not resurrection, showing the natural explanations were the disciples' own first instinct too.

This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. The claim is proclaimed publicly in Jerusalem within weeks of the crucifixion, in the city where the body could have been produced, which the authorities never managed to do.

And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. Paul keeps the whole structure resting on the event, refusing every alternative that would let the faith survive as inspiring fiction if the body stayed dead.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the logic of inference to the best explanation, because it is the actual method of this session and of historical reasoning generally, and misunderstanding it is what lets both believers and skeptics overclaim. Historians do not prove that an event occurred the way a mathematician proves a theorem. They weigh competing explanations of a body of evidence and ask which best accounts for the data, with the fewest strained assumptions, the widest explanatory reach, and the greatest fit with what else is known. N. T. Wright, in The Resurrection of the Son of God, argues that the rise of the early church, with its specific and otherwise unprecedented belief, requires a sufficient cause, and that the empty tomb and the appearances together, each insufficient alone, jointly provide one, while no natural alternative accounts for both. The honest skeptic's strongest move, articulated by Bart Ehrman, is to insist that a miracle, being maximally improbable, can never be the most probable explanation and so can never be the historian's conclusion. Hold these two side by side, because the disagreement is precise and instructive. Wright is asking which explanation best fits all the evidence. Ehrman is arguing that one candidate explanation, the miraculous one, is disqualified before the comparison begins. A serious group should see that this is not finally an argument about the evidence at all but about whether the supernatural is permitted on the table, which is a prior commitment each person brings rather than a finding the evidence yields. Set this beside the principle of Ockham's razor, often invoked by skeptics, which says do not multiply explanatory entities beyond necessity, and ask the hard question fairly: is a single event, however extraordinary, that explains all the facts at once simpler or more complex than a stack of separate ordinary explanations, one for the tomb, another for the disciples, another for Paul, another for James, each straining in its own way. There is no neutral ground here, and the discipline of this session is to admit that openly. The weighing is real and the facts are real, but what a person will accept as the best explanation depends partly on what they were willing, before they began, to allow could be true.
